text: Cowardice keeps a ledger, and the payments fall due on grandchildren who were nowhere near the original act. Julio Medem folds three generations of two Basque families into ninety-six minutes, so whole decades drop out between scenes and what survives the cut is the grudge, the land, and the boundary the two households keep crossing. It is filed in part as a war film, and there is war in it, but the longer fight is the one carried on at close range by people who will still be sharing a valley when it is over. Something in the first generation goes undescribed in the houses that follow, and the children grow up around the shape of it. It sits on Caimán's hundred best Spanish films, a strange address for a story that barely leaves one hillside.

A woman scrubs other people's floors in a building that is losing its own plaster. Maria left the countryside to get out from under her father, and what the city gave her in exchange is a decaying flat, a pregnancy the man refuses to acknowledge, and work paid by the hour. Then the father needs an operation, the operation is in the city, and her mother arrives with a bag and stays. Benito Zambrano keeps it all at kitchen scale: two women in a few square metres, one of them long practised at absorbing a husband's temper and now offering that practice as help. No one makes a speech. The pressure is rent, a shift that can be lost by turning up late, and the sums involved in a birth with no second wage behind it.

The arm comes off early, and the rest is a problem in adaptation: a fighter relearning a craft built for a body he no longer has. Chang Cheh returns him to his old teacher's gate at the moment rivals are closing on it, which makes obligation the subject before combat is - what a man still owes a house that made him, and what the house has ever owed back. A hundred and eleven minutes out of Hong Kong in 1967, and the choreography is asked to argue rather than decorate: technique rebuilt in private, a reputation travelling ahead of its owner, an arrival that reads less as homecoming than as a debt being called in. Every exchange tests whether one hand can be enough. The film keeps arranging conditions in which it very nearly is not.

An inn on a frontier road, soldiers already sitting in it, and children travelling into exile who have to pass through. King Hu fixes the year at 1457 and then narrows the map almost to one building, so the middle of the film is a matter of who sits where, who is served what, and how long two sides can keep up the courtesy of strangers. That patience is the technique. The swordplay arrives as punctuation, quick and finished before the room has rearranged itself, and the rest of the tension sits in seating and service. Taiwan, 1967, a hundred and eleven minutes: an execution ordered in the capital and a sentence of exile, settled at a table where tea is being poured for people who intend to kill each other.

A discharged soldier and a widow, and a great deal of unstructured time between them. Vicente Aranda films the affair that follows as an economy rather than a romance: what each one has to offer, what it costs the other, which of them can still afford to walk. The widow has the room and the standing. He has only just stopped being told what to do, and the freedom turns out to be less useful than he expected. Spain, 1991, a hundred and three minutes, and the crime listed on the file is not decoration - appetite here keeps acquiring practical consequences, and the film watches them accumulate without raising its voice. What holds it together is Aranda's refusal to sentimentalise the bargain. The lovers say love and mean possession, and the camera does not correct them.

A scout running from a battle nobody in it could explain falls through a crack in the mountain and lands in somebody else's war. Tsui Hark starts in the fifth century with civil armies that all look alike to the man fleeing them, then hands that same man a cosmic assignment against something called the Blood Demon, and keeps him a scout throughout: out of his depth, taking orders from adepts whose powers he has no way to assess. The comedy comes from the difference in rank. Ninety-eight minutes, Hong Kong, 1983, and they go on movement, colour and the mechanics of the impossible rather than on explaining any of the rules. The hero stays unqualified. Where everyone else is a master, that is both the joke and the only honest vantage available.

The scheme needs three things: a man nobody will come looking for, a shaft deep enough to make it plausible, and an owner who would rather settle than be inspected. Two miners have turned that into a living. Li Yang films the work without distance - the descent, the dust, the long stretches that have to be got through before anything can happen - so the fraud sits inside a real job rather than beside one. Ninety-two minutes, and most of them are procedure: finding the man, keeping him calm, getting him down. China in 2003 supplies the rest, since the whole arrangement depends on men who travel for work and arrive where nobody knows them. Li Yang lets the sums stand: a life priced as a settlement, and a settlement cheaper than an inspection.

A basket is left at a monastery door, and the monks keep what is in it. Marcelino grows up with several fathers and no mother, an arrangement the house manages well enough until the boy is old enough to notice it; then the loneliness has to go somewhere, and it goes up the stairs to the attic he has been told to stay out of. Ladislao Vajda made the film in 1955, Spanish in its dialogue and Italian in its production, and it is most alive in the ordinary business of the house - the chores, the tolerated mischief, the parenting improvised by committee among men with no children. It carries the Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. The devotional material is open about its intentions; harder to shake is the plainer thing underneath, that a child surrounded by kind adults can still be short of exactly one.

Six years is long enough for a face to become unreliable, which does not stop him. The premise José Luis Guerín sets is thin on purpose: a man, a city he has been in before, a woman he met once and cannot produce a name or an address for. What is left is looking, and the film gives eighty-two minutes to it - a resemblance followed through a crowd, the wrong woman turning around, the mistake at the corner, the return to a table to begin again. Romantic by category and close to surveillance in practice, and Guerín never resolves that discomfort in the man's favour. The terraces, the glass and the traffic of strangers hold more interest than the search does. The search half knows it, which is why he keeps sitting back down.

A man who manufactures door intercoms has bought himself a weekend of aristocrats, and the receipt is the joke. Luis García Berlanga sends this Catalan businessman to an estate outside Madrid with his mistress in the car and a plan to convert one hunting party into a distribution deal, then refuses to let anyone hunt in peace: the estate has an owner, the owner outranks the man who organised everything, and rank keeps reasserting itself over the guest list all afternoon. Ninety-five minutes, a house full of talkers, nobody quite in control of the version of events they are producing. It carries the Medal of the Circle of Cinematographic Writers for best film. The comedy is in the ratio - vast effort spent on proximity to people who can grant favours, and no way anywhere of simply asking.

School is finished in the fishing village and nothing has been arranged to follow it, so the days go on drink, on picking fights, on the harbour. Three of the boys get as far as Kaohsiung, where there is work and an apartment found through somebody's relative, and the city turns out to be less an escape than a change of terms: rent now, hours now, thin walls and neighbours who hear everything. Ah-Ching is drawn to the woman next door, who belongs to somebody. Hou Hsiao-hsien will not share the boys' own sense of drama, letting the same kind of afternoon happen more than once until the repetition carries the meaning. Ninety-eight minutes, 1983, and an island that can be returned to only by admitting the city did not take.

A young woman who has been elsewhere takes a job in a house that has not. Ana arrives at a country manor to look after three girls and finds a household running on rules nobody thought to explain, held in place by adults who have agreed among themselves not to name what is wrong. Carlos Saura made it in Spain in 1973, and his method is to keep the newcomer's eye as the only reliable instrument in the building: what she notices is ordinary until it accumulates, and then it stops being ordinary. A hundred and two minutes inside one property, where the family's authority and its appetites have the run of the place because no one from outside is ever coming. The menace is not violence. It is the assurance of people never once contradicted at home.

The client is dying, and the job he is paying for is easy to state and hard to finish: find the daughter who ran, while there is still someone to bring her to. Germán Areta, called el Piojo, works the trade the way it actually works - waiting, phone calls, favours from people who owe him nothing and answer anyway. José Luis Garci gives him a hundred and twenty-one minutes, long for a detective picture, and spends the surplus on the walking. The case supplies what such cases supply: a young woman who had her reasons for going, and a man who would like to be forgiven by proxy before his time runs out. Spain, 1981. The film is unhurried and cool to the touch, and its interest is the errand rather than the solution.

Two women sit down together after thirteen years apart, and the film gives them a hundred and sixty-six minutes to account for the gap. One has come back from a concert tour in Europe; the other has just opened a business. Edward Yang treats the reunion as a frame and then keeps leaving it, since the talk summons years that arrive in pieces rather than in order, the way anyone actually retells a decision. Taiwan, 1983. What gets examined is the distance between the life a young woman was told to expect and the one she assembled instead, and the examining happens in offices, kitchens and cars rather than at any turning point. The length is the argument: thirteen years will not compress, and Yang will not make them.
